title: Fluency and Accuracy: Two Goals, Two Approaches
brief: Explain the distinction between fluency-focused and accuracy-focused speaking activities, drawing on the module's discussion of how a teacher may choose not to correct oral errors in order to keep the flow of ideas going and help students develop fluency and confidence. Cover the module's point that the goal of an activity or lesson — developing fluency or accuracy — is one of the key factors teachers must consider when planning speaking work. Explain that focusing on content and communication rather than grammatical form is a deliberate pedagogical choice, not an oversight. Do not go into error-correction procedures in depth; that is covered in M9.

title: Lowering the Affective Barrier
brief: Draw on the module's discussion of students' personalities, shyness, and confidence as factors that affect speaking performance. Cover the module's suggestions for reducing anxiety: letting students write or think through their answers before speaking, allowing small-group work instead of whole-class performance, and permitting lower-level students to use L1 during small-group work before switching to English-only for whole-class presentations. Also draw on the module's point that open-ended, student-centered activities are more motivating because students express what they actually think, and that the teacher must create an atmosphere of respect for different points of view.

title: Information-Gap Tasks: Getting Learners Talking Through a Purpose
brief: Use the module's description of Activity C — students ask each other questions from their papers and write down classmates' answers — and Activity F — students then discuss the answers they collected — as the concrete model of an information-gap sequence. Explain how the two-stage design (gathering information, then discussing it) creates a genuine communicative purpose and keeps students talking to each other rather than to the teacher. Connect this to the module's broader point about student-centered classrooms where most class time involves students listening to and speaking with each other rather than the teacher speaking most of the time.

title: Role-Play Tasks: From Problem to Performance
brief: Draw on the module's description of Activity B — students read a short problem and create a role-play to offer a solution — and Activity G — students perform the role-plays they created — as a two-phase role-play model (preparation then performance). Also bring in the TV Talk Show activity from the module, in which hosts prepare questions and celebrity guests brainstorm their characters before the groups present to the class, as a second extended role-play example. Highlight how both examples involve preparation time, creative character or scenario work, and a final performance stage, and note that these activities require both critical and creative thinking according to the module.

title: Managing Speaking Time: Groupings and Interaction Patterns
brief: Use the module's activity table — which maps activities to interaction patterns such as pairs, small groups, small groups presenting to the whole class, individuals speaking in front of the class, and whole-class discussion — to explain how teachers can vary groupings to maximise the amount of time individual students are actually speaking. Draw on the module's point that the teacher's role in a student-centered classroom is to ensure all students have an equal opportunity to interact with classmates. Cover the practical option of having students work in small groups instead of in front of the whole class as a way to increase speaking time and reduce performance pressure simultaneously.

title: A Toolkit of Concrete Speaking Activities
brief: Survey a range of ready-to-use speaking activity formats drawn from the module: the brainstorm-and-survey opener (Activity A, TV viewing habits), the opinion word-card activity (Activity D, students pick a word and give an opinion to the class), the Paraphrase It game (saying the same thing in different ways using varied grammatical structures), and the Word Strings game (players build a sentence word by word from a vocabulary picture card). For each activity, briefly describe the procedure as given in the module and identify what kind of speaking practice it provides — opinion expression, paraphrasing, sentence construction, or discussion. End by noting the module's point that variety of activities is a key planning consideration.
